_meta.purpose: STOF Insecure Deserialization Knowledge Base -- real disclosed patterns for stof/modules/deserialization_tests.py.
sources: PortSwigger -- 'ASP.NET ViewState without MAC enabled' (canonical scanner-issue definition)

Claranet/NotSoSecure -- 'Exploiting ViewState Deserialization using Blacklist3r and YSoSerial.Net', documenting the Dec 2019 Microsoft machineKey-leak campaign against thousands of internet-facing ASP.NET sites
PortSwigger -- Java deserialization guidance on `application/x-java-serialized-object` as a documented Content-Type for Java RMI-over-HTTP / legacy Java web-service endpoints

PortSwigger Web Security Academy -- 'Java deserialization using Apache Commons Collections': the 0xAC 0xED 0x00 0x05 STREAM_MAGIC/STREAM_VERSION header every ObjectOutputStream writes, and its `rO0AB...` base64 prefix, as the standard passive fingerprint for 'is this a serialized Java object' used by Burp's own Java Serialized Object passive check and the Freddy Burp extension
GitHub advisories/CVE-2017-5641 -- Apache Flex BlazeDS `application/x-amf` deserialization RCE, documenting AMF as a Java-serialization-adjacent binary Content-Type worth flagging on discovery

Common industry practice (version-banner fingerprinting): identifying a library's version from response metadata (`X-Powered-By`, `Server`, framework-specific version headers) to check it against known CVEs, without exercising the CVE itself -- the same non-exploiting technique this project's own configuration_tests.py already uses for server version disclosure (TC-017.5)
_meta.key_finding: deserialization_tests.py has a firm, deliberate, permanent design rule: it will never send a real gadget-chain/RCE payload (TC-085.1) or a real DoS payload (TC-085.3) against a live target -- both stay NOT_IMPLEMENTED by design, not by default, and this research did not revisit that boundary. TC-085.2 covers a benign polymorphic-type marker that surfaces a deserialization-shaped error without exploiting it; TC-085.4 covers .NET ViewState with MAC validation apparently disabled via pure structural inspection of an already-crawled page body. This round of research added two more genuinely safe, passive, generalizable patterns: TC-085.5 (does any endpoint's already-captured parameter data or own response Content-Type reveal a serialization format at all -- zero-request magic-byte fingerprinting of already-crawled parameter values, falling back to a single harmless GET's own Content-Type header, never a crafted serialized payload) and TC-085.6 (can a specific serialization library and version be read off a response's own version-banner headers alone -- deliberately built as its own headers-only technique rather than coupled to TC-085.2's error probe, since a header-only check has zero dependency on TC-085.2 ever firing and stays meaningfully separate/non-redundant). Every other deserialization detection pattern found in the literature (Java readObject gadget probes, PHP phar:// triggers, Python pickle __reduce__ markers) requires either a real gadget or an out-of-band callback, both outside this module's safe/passive constraint -- correctly not built.

patterns.generalized_transformation: For every already-crawled page whose HTML contains a `<input type="hidden" name="__VIEWSTATE" ...>` field, check the same response for a sibling `__VIEWSTATEMAC` hidden field. No new request is sent -- this reuses the crawler's already-fetched page bodies.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any .aspx-serving (or otherwise ASP.NET WebForms-shaped) crawled page endpoint that renders a `__VIEWSTATE` field.
patterns.evidence_signal: TRUE signal requires BOTH: (1) `__VIEWSTATE` is present in the page, AND (2) `__VIEWSTATEMAC` is absent from the same response. A page with NEITHER field (non-ASP.NET, or ViewState not used at all) must NOT be flagged -- that's 'not applicable,' not 'vulnerable.' This is a necessary-but-not-sufficient PRECONDITION finding (severity Medium/informational -- 'confirms the precondition for ViewState deserialization RCE', never claimed as confirmed RCE), since full confirmation would require the actual gadget-chain payload TC-085.1 deliberately never sends.
patterns.real_example: PortSwigger's own canonical scanner-issue definition for this exact check; the real December 2019 Microsoft-documented machineKey-leak campaign where thousands of internet-facing ASP.NET sites were found with MAC disabled and exploited via leaked/guessable machine keys plus ysoserial.net (Claranet/NotSoSecure writeup).

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as deserialization_tests.py's _technique_viewstate_mac_disabled, backed by the pure helper _viewstate_mac_disabled(html): for each already-discovered page endpoint (capped at max_endpoints_probed, same cap TC-085.2 uses), a single plain GET via _probe_get (no different in kind from disclosure_tests.py's TC-105.6 page-body scan) is inspected for `name="__VIEWSTATE"` present with no sibling `name="__VIEWSTATEMAC"` in the same body. No exploit/attack payload is ever sent, so this is not gated behind allow_state_changing_probes -- that flag is reserved for real write-verb/attack probes elsewhere in this codebase. A hit reports Finding.severity='Medium' and its description explicitly states it confirms the RCE precondition, never a confirmed RCE. Validated live against this project's real target, demo.testfire.net (Java/JSP, not ASP.NET): TC-085.4 correctly reported PASS across all discovered page endpoints -- no __VIEWSTATE field appeared, which is the honest expected outcome on a non-ASP.NET target, not a shortfall. Unit-tested directly (VIEWSTATE+no MAC -> True, VIEWSTATE+MAC -> False, no VIEWSTATE -> False) plus FAIL/PASS/SKIP integration coverage in tests/unit/test_deserialization_tests.py.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Two-stage, strictly passive check: (1) a zero-request pass over every already-crawled endpoint's `Endpoint.parameter_values`, looking for a value that begins with the Java-serialization magic-byte signature (0xACED0005, hex or its fixed `rO0AB` base64 prefix) -- data STOF already captured, no new request at all; (2) only if that finds nothing, a single harmless GET of an already-discovered endpoint (capped at max_endpoints_probed) whose own response `Content-Type` header is checked against a short list of Content-Type strings that unambiguously name a serialization format (`application/x-java-serialized-object`, `application/x-amf`). No crafted serialized payload of any kind is ever sent in either stage.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any endpoint whose crawler-captured parameter value carries the Java-serialization magic-byte fingerprint, OR any page/API endpoint whose own GET response declares a serialization-format Content-Type.
patterns.evidence_signal: Informational only -- severity='Info', cvss_score=0.0. A hit means 'this endpoint appears to accept/produce a serialization-format payload, worth a manual review', never a confirmed vulnerability claim; there is no plausible false-positive path for the magic-byte check (the 4-byte signature is Java-serialization-specific) and the Content-Type check only matches an explicit, unambiguous serialization MIME type, never a generic `application/octet-stream`.
patterns.real_example: The exact magic-byte heuristic Burp Suite's own passive 'Java Serialized Object' check and the community Freddy Burp extension use to fingerprint a serialized blob without deserializing it; `application/x-java-serialized-object` is PortSwigger's own documented Content-Type for legacy Java RMI-over-HTTP endpoints; `application/x-amf` ties to the real, CVE-2017-5641 Apache Flex BlazeDS deserialization RCE.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as deserialization_tests.py's _technique_content_type_discovery, backed by pure helpers _looks_like_serialized_blob(value) and _content_type_indicates_serialization_format(content_type). Stage 1 (_passive_serialized_blob_hit) needs zero requests -- it only reads Endpoint.parameter_values the crawler already captured. Stage 2 reuses the same authenticated-context/GET shape as TC-085.4/TC-085.2. Never gated behind allow_state_changing_probes since no payload is ever sent. Unit-tested: magic-byte hex/base64 true-positive and ordinary-value false-positive for the pure helper, plus FAIL (passive hit)/FAIL (response Content-Type hit)/PASS/SKIP integration coverage in tests/unit/test_deserialization_tests.py. Validated live against this project's real target, demo.testfire.net (Java/JSP, ordinary JSON APIs): TC-085.5 correctly reported PASS -- no crawled parameter value carried the Java magic-byte signature and no crawled endpoint's own response declared a serialization-format Content-Type, the honest expected outcome for a target that doesn't expose one, not a shortfall.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Headers-only version-banner fingerprint: a single harmless GET of an already-discovered page/API endpoint (capped at max_endpoints_probed), inspecting ONLY response headers (`X-Powered-By`, `X-AspNet-Version`, `X-AspNetMvc-Version`, `Server`) for a known serialization-library name adjacent to a version number (e.g. `X-Powered-By: Jackson-Databind/2.9.8`). Deliberately built as its own separate, headers-only technique rather than piggy-backing on TC-085.2's error probe: a header-only check is strictly simpler, has no dependency on TC-085.2 ever triggering an error, and stays a genuinely independent, non-redundant signal (documented design choice, not an oversight -- see _meta).
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any already-discovered page/API endpoint whose plain GET response carries a version-banner header naming a known serialization library with a version number.
patterns.evidence_signal: Informational only -- severity='Info', cvss_score=0.0. A hit means 'this library/version was disclosed, worth checking against known CVEs for it', never a confirmed vulnerability or exploitation claim. A library name with no adjacent version number is deliberately NOT reported (too weak a signal on its own) -- avoids a false positive on a generic 'Jackson' mention with nothing to check it against.
patterns.real_example: The same non-exploiting 'identify a known-vulnerable library version from response metadata alone' practice this project's own configuration_tests.py already uses for generic server-version disclosure (TC-017.5) -- applied here specifically to serialization-framework version banners (Jackson-Databind, Newtonsoft.Json, fastjson, XStream, .NET BinaryFormatter), which is the real-world first step before checking a disclosed version against, e.g., the many documented Jackson-databind/fastjson polymorphic-deserialization CVEs -- never the CVE exploitation itself.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as deserialization_tests.py's _technique_library_fingerprinting, backed by the pure helper extract_serialization_library_fingerprint(headers) and _LIBRARY_VERSION_RE. Single GET per candidate endpoint, headers dict only (no body/error text ever read -- keeps this genuinely separate from TC-085.2's error-signature probe, not a re-probe of it). Never gated behind allow_state_changing_probes. Unit-tested: known-library+version match, unrelated-header no-match, and name-without-version no-match for the pure helper, plus FAIL/PASS/SKIP integration coverage in tests/unit/test_deserialization_tests.py. Validated live against this project's real target, demo.testfire.net: TC-085.6 correctly reported PASS -- no crawled endpoint's response carried a version-banner header naming a known serialization library with a version number, the honest expected outcome, not a shortfall.
